title: How to Calculate Annual Pay: From Hourly Rates to Lachie Neale's Salary
description: Learn the formula to convert hourly rates to annual salary, including casual loading and super. Understand how it applies to Lachie Neale's salary and award wages.
salarySummary: Using the standard 38-hour week, annual gross pay = hourly rate × 38 × 52. For Lachie Neale's salary, the same formula applies, though his actual earnings are above award rates.

faqs.q: How is annual salary calculated from an hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours worked per week, then by 52 weeks. For a full-time employee on 38 hours, annual gross = hourly × 38 × 52. For example, the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 per hour gives $26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,269.44 per year before tax and super.

faqs.q: What is casual loading and how does it affect pay?
faqs.a: Casual loading is an extra 25% paid on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for lack of paid leave entitlements. Under the National Minimum Wage, casuals get $33.05 per hour ($26.44 + 25%). When converting to annual salary, use the loaded rate if you are a casual employee.

faqs.q: How is superannuation calculated and paid on top?
faqs.a: Superannuation guarantee is 12% of your ordinary earnings, paid by your employer on top of your salary. It does not reduce your take-home pay. For example, on a $52,269 annual salary, super would be $6,272.28 per year, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830.

bodyMarkdown:
## How Annual Pay Works

Whether you're comparing job offers or wondering about Lachie Neale's salary, the core calculation is the same: your annual gross pay equals your hourly rate multiplied by the hours you work each week, multiplied by 52 weeks. This straightforward formula works for award-covered employees, salaried workers, and even high-profile athletes—though their exact figures often come from contracts rather than published rates.

### The Formula

Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52.

For a standard full-time week of 38 hours, the calculation becomes:

Annual gross = hourly rate × 38 × 52.

This assumes you work the same hours every week, with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. It's a starting point for estimating your total earnings before tax and super.

### National Minimum Wage and Award Rates

From 1 July 2026, the National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. That gives an annual gross of $52,269.44. Most employees are covered by an award or registered agreement, which may set higher minimum rates. The Fair Work Ombudsman provides [pay guides](/blog) for each award, updated after the annual wage review. Award minimum wages increased by 4.75% from 1 July 2026.

If you're award-free, the National Minimum Wage applies. For junior employees, apprentices, or people with disability, special rates may apply—see the Fair Work Commission's National Minimum Wage Order.

### Casual Loading

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base rate to compensate for not getting paid leave. For the National Minimum Wage, that's $33.05 per hour. When you use [the timesheet](/), you can check a box to add casual loading. **Do not enter a rate that already includes casual loading**—the tool adds it for you.

If you're a casual working 38 hours at $33.05, your annual gross would be $33.05 × 38 × 52 = $65,336.68. That's significantly higher than the permanent rate, but remember you don't get paid sick leave or annual leave.

### Superannuation Paid on Top

Superannuation guarantee is 12% of your ordinary earnings, paid by your employer on top of your salary. It does not come out of your pay. For the 2026–27 year, the maximum contribution base is $270,830, so super stops once your earnings exceed that threshold.

Using the National Minimum Wage example: annual ordinary earnings of $52,269.44 would attract super of $6,272.33 (12%). Your total remuneration package is $58,541.77, but your take-home pay is based on the $52,269.44 before tax. See [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) for more details.

### Tax and Medicare

Tax is calculated on your gross pay (excluding super). The 2026–27 resident tax rates are:

- $0–$18,200: nil
- $18,201–$45,000: 15c for each $1 over $18,200
- $45,001–$135,000: $4,020 plus 30c for each $1 over $45,000
- $135,001–$190,000: $31,020 plus 37c for each $1 over $135,000
- $190,001+: $51,420 plus 45c for each $1 over $190,000

Medicare levy is generally 2% of taxable income. The low-income thresholds for Medicare reduction are based on 2025–26 figures, as 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed at the time of this estimate. Use [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) to see your net income after tax and Medicare.

### Lachie Neale's Salary in Context

Lachie Neale's salary as an AFL player is not published in official wage databases like the Fair Work Commission or Australian Bureau of Statistics. However, the same formula applies: his annual pay is his contracted hourly rate (or equivalent) multiplied by hours worked per week and weeks per year. Professional athletes often have complex contracts with match payments, bonuses, and image rights, so a simple hourly conversion may not capture the full picture. Still, the principle remains: hourly rate × hours × 52 gives a baseline annual figure.

For most workers, the Fair Work Ombudsman's [pay guides](/blog) and the [minimum wage](/topics/minimum-wage) page provide the rates you need. If you're comparing a salary offer to an hourly rate, use the formula above and remember to add super on top.

### Putting It All Together

Here's a quick example for a permanent full-time employee on the National Minimum Wage:

- Hourly rate: $26.44
- Weekly pay: $26.44 × 38 = $1,004.90
- Fortnightly pay: $1,004.90 × 2 = $2,009.80
- Annual gross: $26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,269.44
- Super (12%): $6,272.33
- Total package: $58,541.77

For a casual employee:

- Hourly rate with loading: $33.05
- Annual gross: $33.05 × 38 × 52 = $65,336.68
- Super (12%): $7,840.40
- Total package: $73,177.08

Remember, these are estimates. Your actual pay may vary based on your award, agreement, or contract. Always check your pay slip and consult the Fair Work Ombudsman if you're unsure.
